title: 3.1.10 Lab: Refactor the Receipt Header
description: The starter prints a repeated header three times. Rewrite it so the header lives in one function, called three times, with the output unchanged. Auto-graded.

steps.title: Spot the repetition
steps.instructions: The starter logs the same header line three times, once before each book. That is the repetition to remove.

steps.title: Define printHeader
steps.instructions: Define a parameterless function called printHeader that logs the header line exactly once, inside the function body.

steps.title: Call it three times
steps.instructions: Replace each of the three inline header logs with a call to printHeader(), keeping the three book lines exactly where they were.

requirements.title: printHeader defined, no parameters
requirements.description: Code defines a function named printHeader with an empty parameter list. Help: 3.1.2 (Defining & Calling a Function)
requirements.hint: Write function printHeader() { ... } with empty parentheses. It needs no input.

requirements.title: header text lives inside printHeader
requirements.description: printHeader()'s body logs the header line. Help: 3.1.7 (Refactoring calcDistance)
requirements.hint: Move the header line into printHeader so the text is written once, inside the braces.

requirements.title: printHeader called three times
requirements.description: printHeader() is called three separate times. Help: 3.1.2 (Defining & Calling a Function)
requirements.hint: Replace each copy of the header line with a call, printHeader();, so the function is called three times.

requirements.title: all three books still printed
requirements.description: The three distinct book titles are still logged, in order. Help: 3.1.2 (Defining & Calling a Function)
requirements.hint: Only the header moves. The three book lines stay where they were, in the same order.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote JavaScript for the lab "3.1.10 Lab: Refactor the Receipt Header". The task they were given: The starter logs the same header line three times, once before each book. That is the repetition to remove. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

questions.r1: printHeader defined, no parameters: Code defines a function named printHeader with an empty parameter list. Code inside a comment, or written inside quotes as text, never runs.
questions.r2: header text lives inside printHeader: printHeader()'s body logs the header line. Code inside a comment, or written inside quotes as text, never runs.
questions.r3: Is printHeader() called three separate times by code that runs? Count the call statements: three written-out printHeader(); calls count wherever they sit, even side by side or inside a block that runs once. This card counts the calls only; whether each header still lands right before its book does not matter here. One call inside a loop that repeats it is not three separate calls. Code inside comments never runs.
questions.r4: Are the three book lines still printed by console.log calls that run, in this order: The Hobbit, then Dune, then Kindred? This card is only about the book lines being kept in order; where the header prints, and how printHeader is written or called, does not matter here. A book line that is commented out does not count. Code inside comments never runs.
